vignette: Mr. Tran, a 69-year-old South Eastern Asian plumber married to his wife of over four decades, has been struggling with symptoms that have progressively worsened over the past year. His experiences during captivity have left indelible marks on his psyche and daily life. Mr. Tran had come to believe that being alone with men triggered intense feelings of nausea and heightened neck pain, which he often experienced while working in tight spaces or at job sites where male colleagues were present. Mr. Tran found himself planning escape routes before entering any new place, a behavior that had become an unconscious habit rooted in his fear of reliving the captivity experience. When reminded of his trauma by certain triggers, such as sudden movements from others, he would feel on guard even inside his own home, and physical reactions like nausea and neck pain would surge forth. His memories of the traumatic event were vivid, playing over and over like a film in his mind. He had come to detach himself from these memories to cope with their intensity, but this strategy only made it harder for him to explain what had happened. When he tried to recount the events, he often lost the thread of his story, unable to find words to describe the experience. The act of detaching from these memories led Mr. Tran to further avoid anniversaries and other reminders that could trigger the intense replaying of traumatic scenes. He was certain that planning escape routes and avoiding male presence provided a sense of safety, but in reality, they only reinforced his feelings of threat. When he encountered sudden movements or felt nauseous, these physical reactions would activate the memory replays, which in turn led to more detachment and avoidance. Over time, this cycle had become increasingly tight, with Mr. Tran's maladaptive strategies and heightened threat perceptions feeding into one another. His work as a plumber often put him in confined spaces and close quarters with colleagues, making it challenging for him to avoid the triggers that set off his distressing symptoms. He found himself withdrawing from social situations and work engagements, leading to strained relationships at home and decreased professional performance. Mr. Tran's wife had noticed these changes over time, urging him to seek help as she watched her husband become increasingly isolated and anxious. What frightened him most was the fear of being trapped again, which he associated with sudden movements or male presence. Despite his best efforts to detach from the memories and plan escape routes, Mr. Tran knew that something had to change. Ultimately, it was a particularly distressing episode at work, where he experienced intense nausea and neck pain while alone with a male colleague in a confined space, that convinced him to seek help. He hoped for a way to regain control over his life without the constant fear of reliving his traumatic experiences. Mr. Tran's journey towards recovery began as he recognized the need to address not just the symptoms but also the underlying mechanisms that kept these memories and fears active in his daily life.
